title: Photonic crystal fiber
title_note: The paper calls it "a new type of optical waveguide: the photonic crystal fiber" and "a novel monomode optical fiber with a hexagonal symmetry" (Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547). It makes no "first" claim. An erratum was published (Opt. Lett. 22, 484 (1997)); it was not read for this story.
tagline: Air holes in silica, stacked and drawn, guide a single mode.

parts.name: silica rod
parts.role: Macroscopic unit cell; one hole drilled down its length.
parts.detail: A hole of 16 mm diameter is drilled down the length of a 30 mm diameter silica rod; six flats are then milled on the outside, forming a regular hexagon. The paper calls the milled rod "this preform". Rod length, silica grade and the flat-to-flat width after milling are not stated (a regular hexagon cut from a 30 mm rod is at most 26.0 mm across the flats, with its corners on the original surface).
parts.quote: We form the hexagonal unit cell on a macroscopic scale by drilling a hole of 16-mm diameter down the length of a 30-mm-diameter silica rod. Six flats are milled on the outside of the rod, forming a regular hexagon.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547 right col.

parts.name: solid cane
parts.role: Cane without a hole; becomes the high-index core.
parts.detail: At the stacking stage one of the hollow hexagonal canes is replaced by a similar cane without a hole in the middle. This purposely introduced high-index defect makes the fiber guide by a reduced effective index of the surrounding silica-air matrix; it does not rely on a complete band gap.
parts.quote: We do this at the stacking stage by replacing one of the hollow hexagonal canes with a similar cane that does not have a hole in the middle.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547 right col.

geometry.note: same outer size as the hollow canes ('similar cane')

parts.name: stack
parts.role: Canes stacked into the hexagonal crystal, solid cane centered.
parts.detail: The paper does not print the cane count. Counted from Fig. 1: complete rings of holes 1 to 8 around the solid core (215 of 216 sites resolved; one site lost at a chipped corner) and a ninth ring at the fiber edge, partly resolved; the outer flats run parallel to rows of holes. Nine rings also follow from the printed widths: 38 µm / 2.3 µm = 16.5 pitches across the flats, and a hexagonal stack of N rings of hexagonal canes is about 2 × (0.87 N + 0.43) pitches across, so N = 9. That makes 271 canes (270 hollow, 1 solid). How the stack was held is not stated; no jacket tube is drawn (the fiber outline in Fig. 1 is hexagonal).
parts.quote: This stack is again drawn on the tower, fusing the stacked canes together and reducing the pitch (center-to-center spacing) to ~50 µm.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547 right col.; Fig. 1 (p.1548)

parts.name: photonic crystal fiber
parts.role: Hexagonal silica fiber with air holes along its whole length.
parts.detail: Fig. 1 fiber: flat-to-flat width 38 µm, pitch 2.3 µm, solid core nominally 4.6 µm wide; the structure is virtually invariant over several meters. Air holes run the entire length of the fiber, which is many meters long. The three-stage draw reduces the unit cell by a factor of more than 10^{4}. Tests used a 1 m length. The fiber is quite robust and easy to handle despite its small size.
parts.quote: The flat-to-flat width of the fiber shown is 38 µm, the pitch is 2.3 µm, and the solid core region is nominally 4.6 µm wide.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547 right col.

parts.name: air holes
parts.role: Hexagonal lattice of holes; lowers the cladding's effective index.
parts.detail: Air holes in a regular hexagonal pattern run the entire length of the fiber. Their relative diameter in Fig. 1 is smaller than in the original unit cell, an effect of surface tension in the final drawing stages; by varying the furnace temperature the authors drew fibers of similar pitch with holes of 0.2-1.2 µm diameter. The Fig. 1 hole size is not printed in this paper; the authors give d/Λ about 0.15 for this fiber a year later (Birks et al., Opt. Lett. 1997, p.962), i.e. about 0.35 µm. A half-depth read of the micrograph gives 0.16-0.20 Λ (blur-limited).
parts.quote: Air holes arranged in a regular hexagonal pattern run the entire length of the fiber, which is many meters long.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1547 left col.

parts.name: solid core
parts.role: Missing hole at the center; the light is confined here.
parts.detail: The solid core region is nominally 4.6 µm wide (two pitches). Light with propagation constant β above a certain value is confined to the core, because the surrounding silica-air matrix has a lower effective index than the solid core.
parts.quote: In this case we expect any light with β greater than a certain value to be confined to the core, as the surrounding silica-air matrix has a reduced effective refractive index compared with the solid core.

parts.role: Far-field pattern photographed a few centimeters from the end.
parts.detail: The far field fell on a sheet of paper several centimeters from the far end of the fiber and was photographed (Fig. 3(a) on p.1549, 632.8 nm; Fig. 3(b) overexposed to show higher-order spots). Independent of launch and unaffected by bends: a single low-loss guided mode. Fig. 3 has no angular scale.

parts.name: guided mode
parts.role: Light confined to the core; minima at the six nearest holes.
parts.detail: Near field at 632.8 nm (Fig. 2(a)): strongly confined to the core, dominated by minima at the six nearest air holes; a factor of 25 between the innermost and outermost contours. Visible light is redistributed into the higher-index silica of the cladding; at long wavelengths the mode stays tightly confined but the cladding acts more like a uniform medium of average index, so its effective index falls sharply. This keeps the V value nearly constant: one robust mode over a wide range.
parts.quote: The light is strongly confined to the core region, and the field pattern is dominated by minima occurring at the six nearest air holes.
parts.locator: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, p.1548 left col.

chapters.line: A hole drilled down the length of a silica rod.
chapters.action: rod rises into view upright, slow quarter turn; a drill bore opens down the axis; label dia. 30 mm, hole 16 mm

chapters.line: Milled on six sides into a regular hexagon.
chapters.action: six flats cut away one after another (thin silica slabs fall off), leaving a regular hexagonal prism with the round hole; flat-to-flat drawn at the 26.0 mm bound (hover says assumed)

chapters.line: Heated on a drawing tower and pulled into thin hexagonal cane.
chapters.action: furnace ring descends around the preform tip and glows; the tip necks down and a thin hexagonal cane with a proportional hole runs downward out of the furnace; cane cut into equal pieces

chapters.line: Hollow canes stacked; one solid cane takes the center.
chapters.action: end-on view: canes fly in ring by ring into a hexagonal close-packed stack (9 rings, 271 canes); the solid cane goes first to the center site, then rings 1 to 9 arrive (order not stated; the paper fixes only the position); outline flats parallel to the rows

chapters.line: Drawn again on the tower, the canes fuse into one rod.
chapters.action: stack enters the furnace; the cane boundaries vanish as it necks down; the drawn rod shows the hole lattice at a smaller pitch; a piece is cut off

chapters.line: A piece of the fused stack is drawn down to fiber.
chapters.action: the fused piece enters the furnace and a hair-thin fiber spools downward; hole size shrinks relative to the pitch during this draw (surface tension); camera follows the fiber

chapters.line: Air holes on a hexagonal lattice around a solid core.
chapters.action: camera dives to the fiber end face; cross-section resolves: hexagonal outline, nine rings of small holes, the missing center hole as the core; pitch label; holes extrude back along the fiber to show they run its whole length

chapters.line: Laser light focused into the core; cladding light stripped.
chapters.action: test bench: laser box, objective, 1 m fiber (drawn coiled or shortened; length labelled), index-matching fluid sleeve near the input; red 632.8 nm beam focuses into the core; light leaking into the cladding fades out at the fluid

chapters.line: Confined to the core, with dips at the six nearest holes.
chapters.action: output end glows red; end-face close-up with the mode shaped by the digitized contours (six dips at the nearest holes); vidicon camera with objective on the axis; the plot assembles: holes first, then contours outermost to innermost

chapters.line: One mode for each laser, blue to infrared (false colour).
chapters.action: camera swaps for the sheet of paper; far-field pattern (central spot plus six spots) appears at one schematic size (Fig. 3 prints no angular scale); the beam colour steps through the four lasers, blue to infrared (850 / 1550 nm in labelled false colour); the pattern keeps its shape and the outer spots weaken slightly toward long wavelengths; the two printed NA values are in the side panel (no NA plot, no line between them)

plots.label: Paper Fig. 2(a)
plots.source: Knight et al., Opt. Lett. 1996, Fig. 2(a) (p.1548): 'Contour plot of the recorded near-field pattern of the guided mode (λ = 632.8 nm) superimposed upon an approximately scaled portion of a scanning electron micrograph'
plots.note: Near field at 632.8 nm, digitized from Fig. 2(a). Contour levels are not printed: the innermost (strongest) and outermost contours differ by a factor of 25 (caption). The micrograph under the contours is only approximately scaled; distances use its hole lattice set to the printed pitch of 2.3 µm, origin at the missing center hole. Stroke centers sampled every 0.06 µm of contour length; where the outer contour runs into a hole the points are dropped and the gaps (up to 0.6 µm) are bridged by straight segments.
